question: It is becoming increasingly clear that large quantities of Russian grain are entering the EU through both Latvia and Lithuania. It is likely that some of this grain has been seized from Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia. Therefore, if we do not bring this transit of grain through the EU under control, it will bolster Russia’s economy and its war against Ukraine.

The quality of this grain is not being checked, and its possible mixing with Lithuanian grain – known for its high quality – will damage the reputation of Lithuanian grain producers. In addition, the aforementioned entry of Russian grain onto the market has likely caused a significant drop in Lithuanian grain prices, while grain elevators are still full.

At the end of 2023, the price of triticale was about 46%, rye about 37% and wheat about 33% lower than in 2022. In other words, grain prices in Lithuania have fallen by a third. In this context, is the Commission aware of this problem and, if so, what measures does it intend to take in order to address these problems, to restore balance on grain markets and to stop supporting the Russian economy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2024) Russia exported 4.2 million tonnes of cereals, oilseeds, and derived products to the EU in 2023, worth EUR 1.3 billion. It must be noted though that imports to the EU remain a fairly small piece of the overall supply picture for these products, with domestic suppliers furnishing 300 million tonnes per year.

However, Russia is a leading world-wide producer of grains and, given its current exports to the world, it could reorient significant volumes of its supplies to the EU. Moreover, Russia is illegally appropriating cereals and oilseeds produced in the territories of Ukraine, which it illegally occupies, and it is routing these supplies to its export markets as allegedly Russian products.

Therefore, on 22 March 2024, the Commission has put forward a proposal for a Regulation increasing the tariffs on imports into the EU of cereals, oilseeds and derived products1 (‘grain products’) including wheat, maize and meals of sunflower seeds from Russia and Belarus.

In addition, Russia and Belarus will no longer have access to any of the EU’s World Trade Organisation quotas on grain that offer better tariff treatment for some products. The increased tariffs are expected to enter into force upon the adoption of the Commission’s proposal by the Council.
